title: One day at a time
hook: Jesus: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof (Matthew 6:34)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child at the edge of a well, and a saying about work you don't have to finish. Your line was not numb. What one thing did you do for a far-off place? Day seven hundred forty-eight.

"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It sounds like something carved over a door in an old courthouse. It is actually the last line of a short talk about worry, in the Gospel of Matthew, and in the story Jesus says it to a crowd on a hillside. The text calls them the multitudes: people with bills, harvests and children of their own to worry about. He doesn't tell them their troubles are imaginary. He tells them something stranger. Today has enough of its own.
screen: `A LINE THAT SOUNDS LIKE A COURTHOUSE.` → `A CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `TODAY HAS ENOUGH OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the King James Bible the passage keeps saying "take no thought." Readers sometimes hear that as don't plan. The talk is about worry, the kind that runs ahead and chews on things that haven't happened. Second, the birds and the flowers. "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them." And then: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." In between, a question with a smile in it: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" Worry, it turns out, doesn't make anyone taller. Third, the closing line in full. "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Evil here means trouble, hardship. Notice what the line admits. Today has trouble. It doesn't promise an easy day. It says one day's share is enough to carry, and tomorrow's share can wait for tomorrow. Fourth, where it sits. The same sermon, a little earlier, holds the prayer Christians call the Lord's Prayer, with its line "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread for this day. Not a year's supply. Some readers hear the two together: trust practiced one day at a time. And the same shape turns up outside the church too, in recovery rooms and hospital waiting rooms: handle today. Just today.
screen: `TAKE NO THOUGHT: A TALK ABOUT WORRY.` · `BIRDS, LILIES, AND ONE CUBIT.` · `SUFFICIENT UNTO THE DAY.` · `BREAD FOR THIS DAY.` · then, large: `TODAY IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the shoulders drop. Bring up whatever is weighing on you. Now sort it, gently. What belongs to today: a call, a meal, a page, one conversation. And what belongs to a later day: the test next month, the bill next season, the thing that might happen. Picture setting the later things on a shelf. They'll be there. You can pick them up on their own day. For now, hold only today's share, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can ask for today's bread and nothing more. The bell holds the time.
One day at a time: carrying only today's share, because, in Matthew's words, sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. Today's word.
screen: `ONE DAY AT A TIME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today is enough. When a worry about next week arrives today, ask whose day it belongs to, and put it back on the shelf. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer each morning, asking for 'this day our daily bread', and turn to Matthew 6 in anxious seasons; recovery groups use the phrase 'one day at a time' in a similar spirit.

fork.setup: it's 2am and a worry about next month shows up. what does Matthew 6:34 point toward?
options: solve next month now, while you're awake.
let tomorrow take thought for itself; today's share is enough.
fork.reveal: "the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." it doesn't deny the trouble; it gives each day its own share.

original.note: Greek: 'sufficient, enough', the first word of 'sufficient unto the day' in Matthew 6:34 (the verse itself opens differently).

trapdoor: what you thought: one day at a time is a slogan from a poster.
what it means: carry today's share of trouble, and let tomorrow carry its own.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 6:25–34, the talk on worry closing the chapter that holds the Lord's Prayer and its 'daily bread' (6:11).

'Evil here means trouble, hardship' (Greek kakia in 6:34): confirm gloss.
